claims.text: A unified framework combining high-throughput ab initio molecular dynamics, CALPHAD, and targeted in situ experiments can predict melting and liquid-phase properties across the high-entropy-alloy family.
Nearly equiatomic multimetal HEAs form complex solid solutions stabilized by high mixing entropy.
Ab initio simulations and CALPHAD can be calibrated using differential scanning calorimetry, in situ TEM heating, and high-temperature diffraction.
Combined in situ STEM heating and molecular-dynamics simulation can resolve atomic-scale thermal evolution and melting phenomena in an HEA nanoparticle.
The proposed approach applies from room temperature through and beyond melting in transition-metal-based HEAs.
Substitution of Co by Cr can significantly alter phase stability in an HEA.
Mixing enthalpy, configurational and vibrational entropy, and diffusion kinetics mediate HEA phase transitions and melting behavior.
Pronounced atomic diffusion can drive temperature-dependent phase separation and surface-layer melting in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Strong local atomic interactions and global thermodynamic behavior jointly govern melting in HEAs.
Calibration against high-fidelity experiments corrects shortcomings of empirical rules and binary approximations and thereby improves predictive accuracy.
The binary Hume–Rothery rule is not directly applicable to complex multicomponent HEAs.
The framework will predict melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, volume change at melting, and liquid-phase properties with errors below ±5% relative to experiment.
The framework will reproduce qualitative compositional trends in phase stability.
Conventional empirical or semi-empirical methods inadequately represent complex multicomponent interactions.
Conventional empirical or semi-empirical methods have larger predictive uncertainties than the proposed framework.
The framework is optimally applicable to bulk, metallic, equiatomic or near-equiatomic HEAs.
Nanoscale effects and substantial elemental segregation beyond the calibration domain may limit the framework.
Nonmetallic bonding environments may limit the framework.
Scarcity of high-temperature experimental data across HEAs makes the precise quantitative improvement uncertain.
Failure to reproduce experimental measurements within ±5% or to capture systematic substitution trends would falsify the proposed approach.
